description: Normative global pathway to net-zero CO2 by 2050 consistent with 1.5°C after mid-century overshoot.
pathwayDescription: The Net Zero Emissions by 2050 Scenario (NZE) is a normative pathway that sets out how the global energy sector could reach net zero CO2 emissions by 2050, recognising that each country will follow its own route. It is consistent with limiting the long-term temperature rise to 1.5°C (50% probability). The 2025 NZE is no longer a limited-overshoot pathway: warming peaks at around 1.65°C around 2050 and stays above 1.5°C for several decades before falling back below 1.5°C by 2100. Getting there requires very rapid deployment of renewables, grids, storage, electrification and efficiency, alongside widespread use of CO2 removal technologies that are not yet proven at large scale. For comparison, the IEA’s Current Policies Scenario (CPS) and Stated Policies Scenario (STEPS) correspond to 2.9°C and 2.5°C of warming by 2100 (50% probability).

coreDrivers.policies: NZE assumes co-ordinated, front-loaded policy action across all major instrument types. Carbon pricing rises materially faster and higher than in the accompanying CPS/STEPS pathways. There are also explicit fossil-fuel and technology phase-out dates, target technology shares, subsidies, and feed-in-tariff-style price support to reach net zero by 2050.
coreDrivers.emissionsTargets: The NZE Scenario is designed and constrained to reach net-zero energy-related CO2 emissions globally by 2050, with a temperature peak at about 1.65°C around 2050 before declining below 1.5°C by 2100. This is a materially higher and longer overshoot than in earlier NZE editions.
coreDrivers.technologyCosts: NZE relies on the fastest and deepest technology cost declines of the three WEO scenarios to support its much larger and faster low-carbon build-out. This includes both for established and innovative low carbon technologies.
coreDrivers.investmentChange: Low-emissions technologies approach 100% of power-sector investment by 2035, with power investment above USD 2.5 trillion a year by 2035, nearly double today. Fossil-fuel supply investment falls from about USD 1 trillion a year to under USD 350 billion in 2035 and 90% below today by 2050.
coreDrivers.macroeconomicDrivers: Population and GDP growth are common assumptions across all three WEO-2025 scenarios (global GDP CAGR 2024-2050 = 2.6%; population rising from 8.09 to 9.57 billion).
coreDrivers.otherDrivers: Widespread deployment of CO2 removal technologies (direct air capture, and other CDR) that are 'currently unproven at large scale' is a distinct, load-bearing NZE assumption. It is what brings the temperature back below 1.5°C by 2100 after the mid-century overshoot.

dependencies.dependency_description: NZE is not feasible without co-ordinated power-sector policy such as carbon prices rising materially faster than CPS/STEPS, explicit coal/gas phase-out, 100%-clean-generation trajectories, and strong target-technology-share and subsidy support. Generation and capacity outcomes go far beyond what current or drafted policy alone would deliver.
Faster interconnection, permitting and market-design reform is implied by the scale and speed of the NZE build-out (e.g. solar capacity nearly doubling relative to STEPS by 2050).
NZE's materially higher and faster-rising carbon prices (Annex B.6) are the central economic lever making the pathway's very large low-carbon investment economically rational at the pace required.
Nuclear capacity grows fastest of the three scenarios, with a large reliance on public acceptance of new nuclear (including SMRs).
NZE depends on rapid uptake of efficient electric end-use technologies and demand-side flexibility to reduce final energy while electricity demand rises.

NZE requires by far the largest battery-storage build of the three WEO2025 scenarios to integrate a power system where solar and wind alone reach roughly 75% of generation by 2050, making storage and grid-flexibility infrastructure a binding enabling condition for the pathway's feasibility.

NZE depends on the fast deployment of technologies not yet fully market-ready. CCUS, green hydrogen/ammonia, enhanced geothermal (EGS/AGS), SMRs, and direct air capture reach market readiness and cost-competitiveness at a pace beyond CPS/STEPS.

NZE's large low-carbon technology build-out (solar capacity 24,530 GW by 2050, battery storage 5,716 GW) implies the largest critical-mineral demand of the three scenarios, directly engaging the report's central 2025 theme of concentrated mineral-refining supply chains as a transition bottleneck.

NZE's very high reliance on variable renewables and continued hydropower (7,398 TWh by 2050) increases exposure to the drought and extreme-weather risks the report flags for hydropower and grid infrastructure generally.

NZE retires the most fossil generation capacity of the three WEO2025 scenarios (coal capacity falling from 2,259 to 381 GW) over the same period, implying the largest fossil-sector workforce displacement and retraining need alongside the largest new low-carbon-sector job creation.

byMetric.scopeLimitations: Combustion emissions from the electricity and heat sectors are combined. Upstream (fuel extraction/processing) emissions are not included. This includes global aggregate power-system output, there is no separate captive or residential-rooftop generation series.
